_comment: Cambridge 0097's Thinking and Working Scientifically and Science in Context objectives for Stage 3 that no Grade 3 unit reached, authored as reasoning prompts. Added 2026-09-17 with the Stages 1-4 re-point, and Stage 3 is where the gap was widest: 0097 makes this the year science becomes something you DO - the five kinds of enquiry are named, measurements go into standard units, results go into bar charts, and an investigation ends with a conclusion - and it publishes 51 objectives against the 2018 framework's 27. THREE were claimed rather than authored, on content that was already there: 3TWSc.02 and 3TWSc.06 in Unit 2, whose separation concept hands the learner a sieve, filter paper, a dish and a jar and asks them to choose, and whose method says 'record what you see for each cup in the table below'; and 3TWSc.03 in Unit 5, which teaches the forcemeter and the Newton. One case went the other way and is worth keeping: 3TWSa.03 (make a conclusion and relate it to the question) is PROMISED by Unit 2's outcome 7 and ticked in its self-assessment, and those two fields are the only places in the unit where a conclusion is mentioned - no method, exploration or worked example asks for one. That is a citation with nothing behind it, so it is authored here rather than claimed.
_vehicle: reasoningPrompts. See cambridge-stage1-enquiry.json for the full note on the deck-only section at Stages 1-4 and why appending is safe.
source: Authored 2026-09-17 against Cambridge 0097 Stage 3, anchored to the investigations in Grade 3 units 1-6.
_minimumCovered: One prompt per Stage 3 TWS/SIC objective that no unit's own content already delivers. Coverage is a number that only goes up.

prompts.prompt: Two children ask a question about seeds. Amina asks 'Are seeds beautiful?' Yusuf asks 'Do bigger seeds grow into taller plants?' Only one of these can be investigated. Which one, and what makes the difference?
keyIdeas: A question you can investigate has an answer you can measure or observe
Beautiful is an opinion, and opinions differ
Yusuf's question names two things you can measure
prompts.modelAnswer: Yusuf's question can be investigated, because you can measure seed size before planting and plant height afterwards, and the numbers would settle it. Amina's question is about an opinion - two people can disagree about beautiful and both be right - so no measurement could ever answer it. A scientific question points at something you can observe or measure.

prompts.prompt: You are going to do the germination investigation in your own kitchen. Write the three safety rules you will follow before you start, and say what each one protects you from.
keyIdeas: Ask an adult before using the stove or hot water
Wash hands after handling soil or seeds
Tie back loose clothing and clear the surface first
prompts.modelAnswer: First, I ask an adult before I touch the stove or hot water, because a burn happens faster than you can pull your hand away. Second, I wash my hands after handling soil, because soil carries germs I could pass to my mouth. Third, I clear the surface and move anything that could be knocked over, so nothing spills on me. Carrying out practical work safely is part of the work, not something you do instead of it.

prompts.prompt: You learned that plants make the oxygen you breathe. Use that one fact to explain why cutting down a large number of trees matters to people who live nowhere near them.
keyIdeas: Plants give off the oxygen animals and people breathe
Fewer plants means less oxygen made and more of the other gas left
Air moves, so the effect is not only local
prompts.modelAnswer: Plants make oxygen while they make their own food, and every person and animal breathes that oxygen in. If a great many trees are cut down, less oxygen is made and more of the gas we breathe out stays in the air. Air does not stay in one place, so the change reaches people far away. Science is how we work out that what we do here has an effect over there.

prompts.prompt: There are five kinds of scientific enquiry: research, fair testing, observing over time, identifying and classifying, and pattern seeking. Your dissolving race is one of them. Which one, and name a question in this unit that would need a different one.
keyIdeas: The dissolving race is a fair test - you change one thing
Sorting materials into dissolves and does not dissolve is identifying and classifying
Watching a soil jar settle for an hour is observing over time
prompts.modelAnswer: The dissolving race is a fair test, because I change one thing - the temperature of the water - and keep the sugar, the stirring and the amount of water the same. 'Which of these ten materials dissolve?' would need identifying and classifying instead, because nothing is changed, things are sorted into groups. And watching a jar of muddy water settle would be observing over time. The question decides the kind of enquiry, not the other way round.

prompts.prompt: Your fair test compares how fast sugar dissolves in cold, warm and hot water. Name the one biggest risk in that investigation and say exactly what you will do about it.
keyIdeas: Hot water scalds
An adult pours the hot water, not you
Use warm from the tap rather than boiling, and keep the cup away from the edge
prompts.modelAnswer: The biggest risk is the hot water, because it can scald skin in a moment and a knocked cup pours it into your lap. So an adult pours it, I use hot water from the tap instead of boiling water from a kettle, and I stand the cup well back from the edge of the table. Naming the risk first is what lets the investigation go ahead at all.

prompts.prompt: Your question was: does temperature change how fast sugar dissolves? Your results: cold 4 minutes, warm 2 minutes, hot 1 minute. Write the conclusion, and make sure it answers the question you actually asked.
keyIdeas: Sugar dissolves faster in hotter water
Say it as the answer to the question asked
Use the numbers as the reason
prompts.modelAnswer: Yes, temperature does change how fast sugar dissolves: the hotter the water, the faster it went - 4 minutes in cold, 2 in warm and 1 in hot. A conclusion is not just 'the hot one was fastest'; it goes back to the question and answers it, and it says which results make you sure.

prompts.prompt: You measured your shadow four times in one day: early morning 180 cm, mid-morning 90 cm, midday 30 cm, late afternoon 150 cm. Describe the pattern in those numbers in one sentence.
keyIdeas: The shadow gets shorter towards midday
Then it gets longer again
Shortest when the Sun is highest
prompts.modelAnswer: The shadow gets shorter and shorter until midday and then grows longer again, so it is shortest when the Sun is highest in the sky. Describing a pattern means saying which way the numbers move, not just listing them.

prompts.prompt: You counted your pulse three times: sitting 80 beats a minute, after walking 100, after running 140. Say how you would set this out as a table and as a bar chart, and what the chart shows at a glance that the table does not.
keyIdeas: Table: one column for the activity, one for beats per minute
Bar chart: one bar per activity, height is the beats
The chart shows the size of the jump
prompts.modelAnswer: The table has two columns, 'What I was doing' and 'Beats in one minute', with three rows. The bar chart has one bar for each activity and the height of the bar is the number of beats. The chart shows at a glance that running raised my pulse far more than walking did - the running bar is nearly twice the sitting bar - which you have to work out for yourself from the table.

prompts.prompt: You took your own pulse today. Name two people whose job is to measure things about the body, and say what they measure.
keyIdeas: A nurse measures pulse, temperature and breathing
A doctor listens to the heart and lungs
Everyone uses science; some people use it at work
prompts.modelAnswer: A nurse measures your pulse, your temperature and how fast you breathe, and writes them down each time so changes show up. A doctor listens to the heart and the lungs to hear whether they are working properly. They are doing what you did with your pulse, with better instruments and more practice - which is what using science professionally means.

prompts.prompt: You could describe how hard you pulled as 'quite hard', or you could measure it with a forcemeter as 3 Newtons. Give two things the Newton lets you do that 'quite hard' does not.
keyIdeas: A standard unit means the same to everyone
You can compare two measurements exactly
Somebody else can repeat your work and check it
prompts.modelAnswer: First, 3 Newtons means the same thing to everybody, everywhere, while 'quite hard' means something different to me than to my father. Second, I can compare exactly: 3 Newtons against 5 Newtons tells me which pull was stronger and by how much, where 'quite hard' against 'very hard' does not. That is the advantage of a standard unit - it travels, and it can be checked.

prompts.prompt: A fridge door shuts with a soft thud and stays shut, and a bicycle stops when you squeeze the brake. Use forces to explain how each one works.
keyIdeas: A magnet in the fridge door pulls on the steel frame
Magnetism works without touching
The brake block rubs the wheel, and friction slows it
prompts.modelAnswer: The fridge door has a magnet along its edge, and it pulls on the steel of the frame - a non-contact force, working across the last little gap, which is why the door pulls itself shut at the end. The brake works the other way: squeezing pushes a block against the moving wheel, and the rubbing is friction, a contact force that slows the wheel down. The same two ideas explain both objects.

prompts.prompt: You want to know how long the Moon takes to go all the way round the Earth, but you cannot watch every night for a month. Where would you research it, and how would you decide whether the answer is trustworthy?
keyIdeas: A book, an encyclopaedia, a museum or a trusted website
Check whether two different sources agree
Compare it with the nights you did observe
prompts.modelAnswer: I would look it up in a science book, an encyclopaedia or a trusted website, and I would check a second source to see whether they give the same number. Then I would compare it with my own record: if I saw a full Moon and then a full Moon about four weeks later, the answer of roughly 29 days fits what I watched. Research is a real kind of enquiry, and checking it against something you observed yourself is what makes it safe to use.

prompts.prompt: Draw a diagram to show why we have day and night. Say which three things your diagram must show, and name one thing you should deliberately leave out.
keyIdeas: The Sun, the Earth, and an arrow for the spin
Mark the lit side and the dark side
Leave out clouds, colours and the stars - they are not part of the idea
prompts.modelAnswer: My diagram needs the Sun on one side, the Earth as a circle, and an arrow showing which way the Earth spins, with the half facing the Sun shaded light and the other half dark - and a dot for where I live, so you can see it move from light to dark. I should leave out clouds, the colour of the sea and the stars, because they are not part of why day becomes night. A diagram keeps the parts that carry the idea and drops the rest.

prompts.prompt: For a very long time most people were sure the Sun travelled round the Earth once a day. Looking at the sky, why was that a reasonable thing to think, and what do we say now?
keyIdeas: The Sun really does appear to cross the sky
You cannot feel the Earth spinning
Now we say the Earth spins and the Sun stays still
prompts.modelAnswer: It was reasonable because that is exactly what it looks like: the Sun rises in the east, crosses the sky and sets in the west, and you cannot feel the ground moving under you at all. We now say the Earth is spinning and the Sun stays where it is, and the Sun only appears to move. Scientific thinking changed because people found better evidence, not because the old idea was silly.
